extracted.intended_audience: OMB staff, federal regulatory reviewers, and agency regulatory economists/analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for OMB and federal agencies on how to measure, analyze, and incorporate the distributional (equity) impacts of proposed regulations into cost-benefit and regulatory decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess regulatory impacts at a granular scale
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should instruct agencies to assess regulatory impacts at as granular a scale as possible, taking into account community demographics and existing risk factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granular measurements can unmask disparities in intensity of regulatory impacts, account for differing exposure levels and vulnerability, and generate more accurate estimates of both benefits and costs. The Equitable Data Working Group's disaggregated data should be used when possible. Granular analyses apply beyond air quality to any policy where population averages may mask disproportionate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer census-block-level geographic units
rubrics_metrics.description: To best assess impacts at a granular scale, agencies should exhibit a preference for census block data rather than larger geographic units such as census tracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing larger units can result in disadvantaged communities being outnumbered by surrounding populations and thereby masked. EPA cautions that pockets of minority or low-income communities may be missed by tract-level analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate varying levels of vulnerability into granular analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Granular analyses should incorporate socioeconomic and demographic risk factors that affect vulnerability (e.g., health status, education) so that identical exposures translate into different health outcomes across groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should use disaggregated dose–response estimates and other risk-differentiated inputs; for example, mortality risk from PM2.5 varies with educational attainment. Incorporating local-level vulnerability can reveal distributional impacts that county-level averages would miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure regulatory costs granularly as well as benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators should seek to estimate both the distribution of regulatory benefits and the distribution of regulatory costs at granular levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs may fall disproportionately (e.g., via job losses, price increases) on particular communities; analysts should model whether firms pass costs to consumers, reduce wages, or change employment. When detailed models are unavailable, employ bounding analyses (short- and long-run scenarios) and compare scenarios using disaggregated data on purchases, wages, and occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide disaggregated totals for demographic subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should provide demographically disaggregated totals of costs and benefits (in addition to aggregate estimates) to evaluate how impacts are distributed across specified subpopulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregated totals enable more rigorous assessment of disproportionate impacts. OMB should encourage agencies to report such subgroup-specific tallies whenever possible to allow decisionmakers to consider distributional consequences alongside aggregate efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB should publish detailed guidance on methodology and subpopulations to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should provide prescriptive guidance to facilitate consistent disaggregated analysis, including a list of subpopulations agencies should consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current executive guidance calls for consideration of distributional effects but lacks technical instruction; OMB's guidance should fill that gap by specifying methodology, recommended demographic categories (e.g., those identified in Executive Order 13,985), and standards for reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative tools to evaluate distributional outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be encouraged to use quantitative tools (for example, inequality metrics and social-welfare-function-based weights) to evaluate distributional outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative measures can help translate disaggregated costs and benefits into metrics that reflect equity considerations. Tools cited include inequality metrics and weights derived from social welfare functions to compare distributions beyond aggregate net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate net welfare using weighted cost–benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could calculate net welfare with weighting schemes that reflect distributional preferences instead of relying solely on unweighted aggregate net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighted cost–benefit analysis allows decisionmakers to capture both efficiency and distributional objectives by upweighting benefits (or downweighting costs) to disadvantaged or highly vulnerable groups according to an explicit social welfare function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitatively assess results of disaggregated analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB could recommend that agencies qualitatively assess and discuss the results of a disaggregated cost–benefit analysis in addition to any quantitative measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where quantitative methods are limited or uncertain, a qualitative discussion of distributional findings (including non-monetized harms such as health effects and human dignity) helps decisionmakers understand equity implications and legal/policy tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop coordinated interagency strategies to identify and compensate disproportionately burdened groups
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should lead whole-of-government approaches to identify groups disproportionately burdened across rulemakings and coordinate use of regulatory and spending authorities to compensate affected communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because distributional burdens can aggregate across multiple rules and agencies, OMB should coordinate between lead agencies and other agencies (including the Domestic Policy Council) and produce regular reports on disparate impacts to facilitate systemwide mitigation and compensation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use EPA and comparable technical guidance to estimate disaggregated health and environmental risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should follow EPA's guidance to estimate health and environmental risks, exposures, outcomes, benefits, and other relevant effects disaggregated by income and race/ethnicity wherever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA guidance contains detailed technical recommendations for assessing environmental justice concerns in national rules; agencies should adopt similar approaches (disaggregation by demographic variables) and leverage existing tools and data sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ fine-scale exposure and transport models with disaggregated demographic data
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses of pollution and other spatially heterogeneous harms should use fine-scale models (e.g., down to one-kilometer or census-block resolution) combined with disaggregated demographic data to estimate local damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows substantial heterogeneity in damages even within counties (e.g., a third of PM2.5 damages within five miles of sources); fine-scale air-transport models and census data are feasible and necessary to identify proximate and distant narrow impact corridors that coarser analyses miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bounding analyses when detailed distributional cost models are not available
rubrics_metrics.description: When models of firm and consumer responses are unavailable, analysts should perform bounding analyses that assume plausible cost pass-through scenarios across prices, wages, and returns to capital in the short and long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing bounding scenarios with disaggregated consumption and income data can shed light on whether a policy is likely progressive or regressive even with limited modeling resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct stakeholder engagement to determine which subpopulations to examine
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of subpopulations to be examined in distributional analysis should be developed through robust stakeholder engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While guidance and executive orders suggest likely subpopulations (e.g., groups identified in EO 13,985), agencies should consult communities and stakeholders to identify relevant local and demographic distinctions to include in disaggregated analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of tax-and-transfer remedies and consider non-monetary harms in regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should consider distributional baselines and non-monetary harms (such as premature mortality) because the tax-and-transfer system may be ill-suited to compensate regulatory losers for non-income-based harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars note that important benefits of regulation (e.g., prevented premature mortality) are not well-addressed by tax-based redistribution. Omitting distributional impacts can mismeasure efficiency; agencies should therefore account for non-monetary harms in distributional assessments.
